items: Two nodes both accepting writes after a partition.
Worse than downtime; the merge is manual and lossy.
Fencing or STONITH prevents it. Nothing repairs it cleanly.
Quorum defends: odd voting members plus a witness.
A minority partition must demote itself, never promote.
Postgres ships no automatic failover at all.
Patroni on etcd or Consul is the de-facto standard.
repmgr or a cloud control plane are the alternatives.
Each node holds a DCS leader key with a TTL.
Lose the key: demote. Hold it: renew. The DCS arbitrates.

lines: # and a clean shutdown of the target node

items: Never just restart an old primary; fence it first.
`pg_rewind` resyncs a diverged node without a base backup.
Surviving standbys: re-point `primary_conninfo` at the leader.
PG12+ can follow across a timeline switch on restart.

blocks.title: Client re-routing options
items: VIP handover, or HAProxy checking `pg_is_in_recovery()`.
A service DNS record with a short TTL.
libpq multi-host with `target_session_attrs`.

blocks.title: Rehearse on a schedule
blocks.text: The failover you have never tested is the failover that discovers your `pg_hba.conf` has no line for the new node.

items: Slots guarantee retention and risk a full disk.
`wal_keep_size` is best-effort and risks a broken replica.
`max_slot_wal_keep_size` is the middle ground.
Streaming is low-latency; archive recovery is the batch fallback.
Fewer, larger checkpoints, and `wal_compression` on FPIs.
UNLOGGED tables for scratch data: no WAL at all.
Avoid blanket UPDATEs of unchanged columns.
Lower `fillfactor` to earn HOT updates.

blocks.title: UNLOGGED is a trapdoor
blocks.text: Fast because nothing is logged: truncated on crash and never present on any replica. Scratch data only.

items: `max_wal_size` + `wal_keep_size` + slot slack + archive backlog.
Give it its own volume when I/O actually matters.
`wal_level = minimal` unlocks COPY tricks, forbids replication and PITR.
Almost never worth it on a production cluster.
Each walsender is a process plus a network stream.
Beyond a handful of replicas, cascade instead of fanning out.
An async replica is a full hardware copy for zero write gain.
Justify it with reads, DR, or backup offload.
Measure each with `write_lag`, `flush_lag`, `replay_lag`.
Blame the network only once the numbers say so.
One 50 GB DELETE spikes WAL and stalls logical decoding.
Batch big transactions or every replica lags behind them.

blocks.title: Write scaling is elsewhere
items: Streaming replication scales reads, full stop.
Citus, BDR, pglogical for sharding or multi-master.
Picking one is a product decision, not a GUC.

blocks.title: Consistency model
blocks.text: Single primary plus physical replication: strong on the primary, eventual on replicas, monotonic within any one replica.

items: Stale slot after decommissioning a replica: `pg_wal` fills, primary PANICs.
`archive_command` returning 0 on failure: PITR silently impossible.
No alert on `wal_status = 'lost'`: that consumer needs a rebuild.
`pg_basebackup` with no `-X stream` and no slot on a busy primary.
One sync standby under `FIRST 1`: its reboot hangs every commit.
Assuming a replica is caught up before you promote it.
Restarting an old primary after failover: split brain. Fence first.
`max_standby_streaming_delay = -1`: one analyst stalls DR replay.
A table with no primary key: replica-identity error on UPDATE.
DDL applied only on the publisher: the apply worker stalls.
`hot_standby_feedback` plus idle-in-transaction: bloat and wraparound.

blocks.title: Check before you promote
blocks.text: Compare `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()` on the standby against the primary's `pg_current_wal_lsn()`. Bytes behind is the data you are about to lose.

lines: -- alert long before the volume fills

items: Segments are 16 MB, so file count times 16 is the size.
Alert on a threshold, never on 100% full.
`pg_wal` growth is the signal that precedes the PANIC.
An inactive ==replication slot== pinning `restart_lsn`.
A failing `archive_command`: unarchived segments never recycle.
Checkpoints falling behind: `max_wal_size` is only a **soft** target.
A large `wal_keep_size` held for every replica.

blocks.title: Tip: quiet clusters and RPO
blocks.text: Set `archive_timeout` so a low-traffic primary switches segments; otherwise up to 16 MB of WAL sits unarchived.

blocks.title: Alert set to ship day one
items: Replica lag, in bytes and in seconds.
Slot retained WAL plus `wal_status`.
`pg_stat_archiver` failure count.
`pg_wal` directory size on disk.
A high requested ratio means `max_wal_size` is too small.
Raising `checkpoint_timeout` cuts full-page-write volume.
`checkpoint_completion_target` spreads the flush, not the work.
`archive_command` must return **nonzero** on failure so Postgres retries.
Never overwrite: `test ! -f dst && cp src dst` is the minimum.
`last_failed_wal` names the exact segment that is stuck.
Alert on ==bytes== behind and on `replay_lag` seconds.
Idle primary: bytes stay flat while seconds look stale.
Check `pg_stat_wal_receiver` on the replica when rows vanish.
An active slot cannot be dropped: stop the consumer first.
Space returns only after the next checkpoint recycles segments.
Set `max_slot_wal_keep_size` so the next one caps itself.

blocks.q: Disk at 98%, pg_wal enormous, primary about to die?
a_bullets: Check `pg_replication_slots` for an inactive slot first.
Drop it if that consumer is truly gone; space frees at checkpoint.
Then check `pg_stat_archiver.failed_count` for a broken archive.

items: Compare `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()` against the primary.
**Fence** the old primary: it must not accept writes.
Promote with `pg_promote()`, not a trigger file.
Re-point other standbys' `primary_conninfo` at the leader.
`pg_rewind` the old primary before it rejoins.

blocks.title: Switchover vs failover
blocks.text: Switchover: stop writes, wait for full catch-up, promote — lossless. Failover is unplanned and may lose async commits.

blocks.title: Tip: bound the blast radius
blocks.text: `max_slot_wal_keep_size` turns an unbounded outage into a bounded loss: the slot is invalidated as `wal_status = 'lost'` and that consumer rebuilds.

blocks.title: The whole handbook in one line
blocks.text: WAL is the ledger: fsync it before the page, stream it to somebody else, and never let a forgotten slot or a broken archive fill the disk.

caption.text: Part 2 of POSTGRES FIELD HANDBOOK. Most Postgres outages are not the query planner — they are a forgotten replication slot quietly eating the disk until the primary PANICs. This handbook walks the whole durability path: WAL records and LSNs, checkpoints and full-page writes, streaming replicas, the five synchronous_commit levels, slots, logical decoding, recovery conflicts, and failover without split brain. Ten pages of field notes, including the three checklist queries worth pinning above your monitor.
